questions.q: What format does this lesson use to run a retrospective on your own capstone build?
options: A formal legal audit
The same three questions from Lesson 28's Post-Incident Activity phase: what happened, what worked, what would you change
A customer satisfaction survey
A CVSS scoring worksheet
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly reuses the Post-Incident Activity structure from Lesson 28 — applied to your own build instead of a live incident.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is an interviewer primarily checking for when reviewing this capstone?
options: Whether the YAML syntax is perfectly valid
Whether you can explain the reasoning behind design decisions, like stage order and the gate threshold
Whether you memorized every CVE number mentioned in the course
Whether the pipeline uses a specific named vendor tool
questions.explain: The lesson draws a distinction between 'it works' and 'it's explainable' — interviews and portfolio reviews mainly test whether you can justify the why behind your choices, not just whether the artifact runs.

questions.q: What is the first part of the four-part structure recommended for presenting the capstone?
options: The trade-off you made
The problem — order-service's original state, with zero automated checks and a stale deploy identity
What you'd do with more time
The exact CVSS formula
questions.explain: The recommended structure opens with the problem, then moves to the design, a concrete trade-off, and what you'd do with more time.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say naming a real trade-off is a stronger answer than claiming the design was perfect?
options: Because interviewers always prefer negative answers
Because it shows you understand why a decision is a trade-off under real constraints, not just that you followed a checklist
Because perfect designs are not allowed in this course
Because trade-offs are required by PCI-DSS
questions.explain: The strongest answer demonstrates understanding of the constraint behind a decision — like a CVSS 9.0 threshold being a tunable starting point — rather than pretending no trade-offs exist.

questions.q: Which topics does the lesson name as deliberately out of scope for 'what you'd do with more time,' rather than things that were forgotten?
options: SAST and dependency scanning
Runtime security, a full SIEM, and broader coverage beyond one service
The policy gate and the deploy identity
The secrets scan
questions.explain: These were the same items Lesson 29 flagged as intentionally excluded to keep the capstone finishable — naming them explicitly as future work shows deliberate scoping, not oversight.
